    User to main agent: "/skill:load-context and explore the following subdomains: the public REST API and the data layer. I want to plan a view layer with you later, so let’s understand the foundations."
    Main agent spawns a sub-agent and prompts it: "Read CLAUDE.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, docs/webserver/API.md, docs/data/architecture.md, server/api.py, server/db.py, and summarize how the REST API and data layers work. Cover how function `server/api.py:from_db` fetches the data by calling the `server/db.py:get_data` function, and how [...proceeds to prescribe ironically specific locations to “discover”]"
    </negative-example-2>
    <positive-example-2 why-good="main agent recognizes the work can be distributed concurrently, shortly shares the wider context (the “why”), replicates the context-gathering levers the user used, and does not micro-manage the agents with how-exactly instructions">
    User to main agent: "/skill:load-context and explore the following subdomains: the public REST API and the data layer. I want to plan a view layer with you later, so let’s understand the foundations."
    Main agent fans out research scope horizontally to two parallel sub-agents and prompts them: "/skill:load-context. The user an I are planning a new view layer, so we need a thorough understanding of the [to one agent] public REST API [to the other agent] data layer. [to both] Study it deeply and exhaustively."
    [Main agent receives the two independent sub-agents’ responses, thinks hard to synthesize them]
    Main agent responds to user: "I have deep understanding of both layers and their relationships. What did you have in mind?"
    </positive-example-2>

3. Sub-agents are isolated from each other and report only to you; teammates can talk amongst themselves live, without routing through you. So spawn a *team* when that live interaction would add value through synergy, the classic case being a GAN-inspired adversarial pairing (planner–reviewer, implementer–reviewer) where one produces and the other pokes holes until both are content. Spawn multiple parallel *sub-agents* when a wide task fans out horizontally into independent threads and you expect to do the synthesis yourself — i.e. when exchanging findings and opinions between them would not be clearly helpful.

4. Since teammates talk to each other, tell each of them to load the this skill (`instruct-other-ai`) on top of the context-gathering skill. If you are spawning an adversary among them, tell it to load the `peer-review` skill too.

    Example 3 settings: the main session loaded `load-context`, explored the code, and the user approved a plan to add rate limiting to the public REST API.

    User to main agent: "Great, go ahead and build it."
    Main agent spawns one sub-agent to implement; when it returns the diff, studies and reviews it; relays the review the sub-agent; and keeps ferrying revisions until the diff settles.

    Main agent spawns an implementer–reviewer team and prompts them: "/skill:load-context, then load `instruct-another-ai`. You are in a implementer–reviewer team. Here is the initial task the user has sent me, verbatim, so you understand the bigger picture: <the-user-message-describing-the-task>. [to the implementer] You implement the plan. Ping your teammate when you think you are done writing. [to the reviewer] You review your teammate’s work when it pings you. Also load `peer-review`. [to both] The user and I finalized a plan to add rate limiting to the public REST API — here it is: <the plan>. Build it and tear it apart amongst yourselves until you are confident it is the simplest working, correct solution faithful to the plan."
    [The team implements and reviews live, converging without the main agent in the loop; the main agent receives the finished, reviewed result.]
    Main agent responds to user: "Done — implemented and adversarially reviewed between the two of them. Here’s what landed: …"
    </positive-example-3>

5. Subagents can take a long time to run - use a 20-minute timeout.

218	        self, flags: ConversationFlags, tool_id_map: dict[str, str] | None = None
219	    ) -> list[MessagePart]:
220	        """Yield all visible content parts based on flags.
221	
222	        This is the single source of truth for:
223	        - What content is visible (flag-based filtering)
224	        - Content ordering (text, thinking, tools, plan)
225	        - Shortening: every payload (text, thinking, plan, tool input/output) is
226	          shortened at the source before rendering, so scaffolding stays out of the budget
227	
228	        Plans are represented as TOOL parts with name="ExitPlanMode".
229	        """
230	        parts: list[MessagePart] = []
231	
232	        # Subagent task prompt — always shown (it is what was handed to the agent).
233	        if self.subagent_task:
234	            parts.append(MessagePart(MessagePartKind.SUBAGENT_TASK, self.subagent_task))
235	
236	        # Text content
237	        if self.text:
238	            text = (
239	                shorten_data(self.text, max_chars=flags.shorten_max_chars)
240	                if flags.shorten
241	                else self.text
242	            )
243	            parts.append(MessagePart(MessagePartKind.TEXT, text))
244	
245	        # Thinking block
246	        if flags.show_thinking and self.thinking:
247	            should_shorten_thinking = flags.shorten or flags.shorten_thinking
248	            thinking = (
249	                truncate_middle(self.thinking, max_len=flags.shorten_max_chars)
250	                if should_shorten_thinking
251	                else self.thinking
252	            )
253	            parts.append(MessagePart(MessagePartKind.THINKING, thinking))
254	
255	        # Tools
256	        if flags.show_tools and self.tools:
257	            self._append_tool_parts(parts, flags, tool_id_map)
258	
259	        # Plan (as tool-like part with name="ExitPlanMode")
260	        if flags.show_plans and self.plan:
261	            plan_content = (
262	                shorten_data(self.plan, max_chars=flags.shorten_max_chars)
263	                if flags.shorten
264	                else self.plan
265	            )
266	            plan_parts = ToolParts(
267	                tag=ContentBlockType.TOOL_INPUT.value.xml_tag,
268	                attrs=[("name", "ExitPlanMode")],
269	                content=plan_content,
270	                is_empty=False,
271	            )
272	            parts.append(MessagePart(MessagePartKind.TOOL, plan_parts))
273	
274	        return parts

329	        """Render one visible message to structured JSON data."""

331	        if not content:
332	            return None
333	
334	        payload: dict[str, object] = {
335	            "type": self.get_wrapper_type().value.xml_tag,

350	        if self.agent_id:

352	            if self.subagent_type:

360	    def _iter_visible_tools(
361	        self,
362	        flags: ConversationFlags,
363	        id_map: dict[str, str],
364	    ) -> Iterator[dict]:
365	        """Yield each visible tool dict, shortened at the source when asked.
366	
367	        Shortening once here — on the raw tool dict via shorten_data — is the single
368	        shortening point for tools, mirroring how text, thinking and plans are
369	        shortened at the source. tool_to_parts/tool_to_json then build their views
370	        (XML content, the colored diff/highlight, JSON) from already-short data, so
371	        no representation can be left untruncated.
372	        """
373	        for tool in self.tools:
374	            show, filter_short = self._should_show_tool(tool, flags.show_tools, id_map)
375	            if not show:
376	                continue
377	            if flags.shorten or filter_short:
378	                tool = shorten_data(tool, max_chars=flags.shorten_max_chars)

406	        """Return a tool id map, building a local one only when needed."""

409	            isinstance(filter_value, list)
410	            and not tool_id_map

412	        ):

415	        for tool in self.tools:

429	    def has_content(self) -> bool:
430	        """Check if message has any displayable content."""

433	        )

435	    def get_wrapper_type(self) -> ContentBlockType:
436	        """Return the XML wrapper type for this message.
437	
438	        agent_id takes precedence over role so that every message belonging to a
439	        subagent (including its tool-result `user` entries) renders as one block.
440	        """
441	        if self.wrapper_type is not None:
442	            return self.wrapper_type

451	    def get_header(self) -> str | None:
452	        """Return the wrapper header, enriched with the subagent nickname when present.
453	
454	        A user-initiated `/fork` (subagent_type "fork") is labelled `Fork` to set it
455	        apart from agent-initiated `Task` subagents, which stay `Agent`.

8	def truncate_middle(s: str, max_len: int = 500) -> str:
9	    """Shorten a string by replacing its middle with an ellipsis block."""
10	    placeholder = "\n...\n"
11	    if max_len < len(placeholder):
12	        placeholder = "..."[:max_len]
13	
14	    if len(s) <= max_len - len(placeholder):
15	        return s
16	
17	    if max_len <= len(placeholder):
18	        return placeholder[:max_len]
19	
20	    remaining = max_len - len(placeholder)
21	    first_half = remaining // 2 + (remaining % 2)
22	    second_half = remaining // 2
23	
24	    return s[:first_half] + placeholder + s[-second_half:]

27	def shorten_data(data: Any, max_chars: int = 500) -> Any:
28	    """Recursively shorten every string leaf in ``data`` to ``max_chars`` characters.
29	
30	    The limit is per string, applied to each leaf as the structure is traversed; it
31	    does not bound the total size of the object (an object with many keys can still
32	    exceed ``max_chars`` many times over).
33	    """
34	    if isinstance(data, dict):
35	        return {k: shorten_data(v, max_chars) for k, v in data.items()}
36	    if isinstance(data, list):
37	        return [shorten_data(item, max_chars) for item in data]
38	    if isinstance(data, str):
39	        return truncate_middle(data, max_len=max_chars)
40	    return data

47	    Content may be a string, list of content blocks ({"type": "text", "text": "..."}),
48	    or other. Returns list of text strings (may be empty).
49	    """
50	    if isinstance(content, str):
51	        text = content.strip() if strip else content
52	        return [text] if text else []
53	
54	    if isinstance(content, list):
55	        texts = []
56	        for item in content:

59	                text = text.strip() if strip else text

62	            elif isinstance(item, str):

88	    (3600.0, "m"),

96	def humanize_age(then: datetime, now: datetime | None = None) -> str:
97	    """Render the age of ``then`` as a compact token like ``24m`` or ``2w``.
98	
99	    >>> base = datetime(2026, 6, 15, 12, 0, 0)
100	    >>> humanize_age(datetime(2026, 6, 15, 11, 59, 30), base)
101	    'now'
102	    >>> humanize_age(datetime(2026, 6, 15, 11, 36, 0), base)
103	    '24m'
104	    >>> humanize_age(datetime(2026, 6, 15, 9, 0, 0), base)
105	    '3h'
106	    >>> humanize_age(datetime(2026, 6, 14, 12, 0, 0), base)
107	    '1d'
108	    >>> humanize_age(datetime(2026, 6, 1, 12, 0, 0), base)
109	    '2w'
110	    >>> humanize_age(datetime(2026, 1, 15, 12, 0, 0), base)
111	    '5mo'
112	    >>> humanize_age(datetime(2024, 6, 15, 12, 0, 0), base)
113	    '2y'
114	    """
115	    seconds = ((now or datetime.now()) - then).total_seconds()
116	    if seconds < 60:
117	        return "now"
118	    divisors = (1, 60, 3600, 86400, 7 * 86400, 30 * 86400)
119	    for (ceiling, unit), divisor in zip(_AGE_UNITS, divisors):
120	        if seconds < ceiling:
121	            return f"{int(seconds // divisor)}{unit}"
122	    return f"{int(seconds // (365 * 86400))}y"
123

125	def age_style(then: datetime, now: datetime | None = None) -> str:
126	    """Return the theme style token for an age, brightest for the most recent.
127	
128	    >>> base = datetime(2026, 6, 15, 12, 0, 0)
129	    >>> age_style(datetime(2026, 6, 15, 9, 0, 0), base)
130	    'search.age.now'
131	    >>> age_style(datetime(2026, 6, 12, 12, 0, 0), base)
132	    'search.age.week'
133	    >>> age_style(datetime(2026, 5, 20, 12, 0, 0), base)
134	    'search.age.month'
135	    >>> age_style(datetime(2025, 6, 15, 12, 0, 0), base)
136	    'search.age.old'
137	    """
138	    seconds = ((now or datetime.now()) - then).total_seconds()
139	    if seconds < 86400:
140	        return "search.age.now"
141	    if seconds < 7 * 86400:
142	        return "search.age.week"
143	    if seconds < 30 * 86400:
144	        return "search.age.month"
145	    return "search.age.old"

148	def elide_to_width(text: str, width: int, *, where: str = "tail") -> str:
149	    """Shorten ``text`` to ``width`` columns on a single line with an ellipsis.
150	
151	    >>> elide_to_width("hello world", 20)
152	    'hello world'
153	    >>> elide_to_width("hello world", 8)
154	    'hello w…'
155	    >>> elide_to_width("/a/very/long/path/here", 12, where="middle")
156	    '/a/ver…/here'
157	    """
158	    if len(text) <= width:
159	        return text
160	    if width <= 1:
161	        return "…"[:width]
162	    available = width - 1
163	    if where == "middle":
164	        left = (available + 1) // 2
165	        right = available // 2
166	        return text[:left] + "…" + (text[-right:] if right else "")
167	    return text[:available] + "…"

70	                combined = style + highlight if style else highlight

I have a complete and verified picture. Let me write up the findings.

## Review findings

I reviewed both commits against their parents, read the full data path (`model.py` → `tools.py`/`parts.py` → `formatting.py` colored renderer + XML renderer, and `utils.py`), traced how every `ToolParts` field is consumed, and confirmed the suite is green on `main`. The two commits are clean and the central abstraction (`shorten_data` as the single shortening point, each renderer formatting already-shortened data) is sound. I went hunting for the adjacent "tetris blocks" you suspected. Most of your candidates turned out to be load-bearing, not collapsible — I'll say why below so you can stop wondering about them. I found one safe deletion.

### The one finding I'm confident about: delete the `_should_show_tool` wrapper

In `src/chats/model.py`, the method at lines 420–427:

```python
def _should_show_tool(self, tool, filter_value, id_map) -> tuple[bool, bool]:
    """Determine if a tool should be shown and whether to shorten it."""
    return resolve_tool_visibility(tool, filter_value, id_map)
```

is now a pure pass-through. It forwards all three arguments unchanged to `resolve_tool_visibility` (already imported in `model.py`) and adds nothing. After your first commit collapsed the two former tool loops into the single `_iter_visible_tools`, this wrapper has exactly **one** caller (line 374). The collapse is: inline it at the call site so line 374 reads `resolve_tool_visibility(tool, flags.show_tools, id_map)` directly, and delete the method. It removes a method and an indirection hop with zero behavior change — the call is byte-for-byte identical. `forking.py` already calls `resolve_tool_visibility` directly six times, so this also makes `model.py` consistent with the rest of the codebase rather than the lone site that routes through a private alias.

That is the whole list. The rest of what follows is me clearing your other candidates so you don't keep poking at them.

### Candidates I checked and am deliberately *not* flagging

**The `tool→parts` vs `tool→json` split is real duplication but not safely collapsible.** `tool_to_parts` and `tool_to_json` produce genuinely different shapes for different consumers: `tool_to_parts` builds fenced-markdown `content` plus the structured side-fields the colored renderer needs, while `tool_to_json` flattens `input_data` into the payload's top level (with conflict-key handling via `payload.update(input_data)`) for machine-readable JSON. Unifying them would mean inventing one intermediate both can derive from — that is *adding* an abstraction, not removing one, and it would risk the JSON golden output. Correctly left alone.

**The `ToolParts` structured fields (`input_data`, `output_text`, `tool_use_id`, `name`) are all still consumed and not redundant with `input_by_id`.** I traced each in `formatting.py`: `input_data` drives the Edit diff (line 226), `output_text` drives the Read syntax highlight (line 238), `tool_use_id` keys the `input_by_id` lookup (line 228), `name` selects the body renderer. They are not duplicated by `input_by_id` — that map holds *input-side* tool dicts so a tool *result* can find its sibling input's file path; `input_data` is the tool's *own* input. Different roles. No safe merge here.

**`output_text` vs `content` on a tool_result looks like double-storage but isn't safely dedupable.** `_tool_result_to_parts` keeps the raw text (`output_text`) and the fenced form (`content`). You could in principle derive raw from fenced by stripping the fence, but that is fragile string surgery introduced to save one field — more complexity, not less, and it would touch the colored Read path that the golden tests pin. Not worth it.

**The `forking.py` per-provider shortening is not the same mechanism and cannot fold into `shorten_data`-at-the-source.** Forking rewrites provider-native transcript JSON in place (Claude/Pi/Codex each have different envelope shapes, plus the Codex case that re-parses JSON-in-a-string), so it must shorten the *original* nested fields, not a normalized `Message`. It already routes everything through `shorten_data`/`truncate_middle`; there is no shared upstream point both it and the renderer could hang off without merging two unrelated traversals. The second commit's rename correctly reached all of these, which is the right scope.

One note worth your attention, not a simplification: `truncate_middle` and `shorten_data` now take differently-named limit parameters — `max_len` and `max_chars` respectively — for the same concept, and `shorten_data` calls `truncate_middle(data, max_len=max_chars)` to bridge them. The rename deliberately stopped at `shorten_data` and left `truncate_middle` as the generic primitive, which is a defensible line. I'm flagging it only because if you ever want the names fully consistent, `truncate_middle`'s `max_len` is the remaining odd one out — but renaming it ripples into every `truncate_middle` caller across `model.py` and `forking.py`, so it's a judgment call, not a clear win.

The Opus reviewer (fresh context, full suite verified green) found exactly one high-confidence, behavior-preserving collapse, and I've applied it.

## Applied — committed `72d9176`

After the shortening unification routed both tool paths through `_iter_visible_tools`, the private `_should_show_tool` method was left as a pure pass-through: one caller, forwarding all three arguments unchanged to `resolve_tool_visibility`. I inlined the call and deleted the method. Zero behavior change, full suite green, and it makes `model.py` consistent with `forking.py`, which already calls `resolve_tool_visibility` directly. A small dead-indirection tetris block, now cleared.

## Cleared — the rest is load-bearing, not collapsible

The reviewer chased the adjacent candidates I was suspicious of and confirmed they should stay, which is useful to know so we stop circling them:

- **`tool_to_parts` vs `tool_to_json`** are genuinely different shapes for different consumers (fenced markdown + structured side-fields for the renderers, versus a flattened machine-readable payload for JSON). Unifying them would *add* an intermediate abstraction and risk the JSON output — the wrong direction.
- **The `ToolParts` structured fields** (`input_data`, `output_text`, `tool_use_id`, `name`) are each still consumed by the colored renderer for distinct jobs, and `input_data` is not redundant with `input_by_id` — that map holds a result's *sibling input*, while `input_data` is the tool's own input.
- **`output_text` vs `content`** on a result could in theory be derived one from the other, but only via fragile fence-stripping that adds complexity to save a field.
- **`forking.py`'s per-provider shortening** rewrites provider-native nested JSON in place, so it can't hang off the same source-shortening point as the renderer; it already routes everything through `shorten_data`/`truncate_middle`, which the rename correctly reached.

## One standing note (not a change)

The reviewer independently raised the `max_len`/`max_chars` naming split — `shorten_data(max_chars=…)` bridging to `truncate_middle(max_len=…)` — as the remaining inconsistency, same judgment call I flagged earlier. It's defensible as-is (`truncate_middle` is the generic string primitive), and fully unifying it ripples into every `truncate_middle` caller. Still your call if you want it; I'd lean toward leaving it.

Three commits now sit on `main`: the source-shortening unification, the `width`→`max_chars` rename, and this wrapper deletion.

1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	"""
3	Truncate long string values in a JSON file or from stdin.
4	
5	Reads JSON from a file or stdin and recursively processes it to middle-truncate
6	any string values longer than 200 characters with "..." placeholder.
7	"""
8	
9	import argparse
10	import json
11	import sys
12	from pathlib import Path
13	from typing import Any
14	
15	
16	def truncate_string(text: str, max_length: int = 200) -> str:
17	    """
18	    Middle-truncate a string if it exceeds max_length.
19	
20	    Args:
21	        text: String to potentially truncate
22	        max_length: Maximum allowed length (default: 200)
23	
24	    Returns:
25	        Original string if under max_length, otherwise middle-truncated version
26	    """
27	    if len(text) <= max_length:
28	        return text
29	
30	    # Calculate lengths for start and end portions
31	    # Reserve 3 chars for "..."
32	    available = max_length - 3
33	    start_len = available // 2
34	    end_len = available - start_len
35	
36	    return f"{text[:start_len]}...{text[-end_len:]}"
37	
38	
39	def process_value(value: Any, max_length: int = 200) -> Any:
40	    """
41	    Recursively process a JSON value, truncating strings as needed.
42	
43	    Args:
44	        value: Any JSON-compatible value (dict, list, str, int, float, bool, None)
45	        max_length: Maximum string length before truncation
46	
47	    Returns:
48	        Processed value with truncated strings
49	    """
50	    if isinstance(value, dict):
51	        return {key: process_value(val, max_length) for key, val in value.items()}
52	    elif isinstance(value, list):
53	        return [process_value(item, max_length) for item in value]
54	    elif isinstance(value, str):
55	        return truncate_string(value, max_length)

58	        return value

content:
That grep surfaced one genuinely related thing, but it's a deliberate non-target. Here's the breakdown:

**All in-package shortening is renamed** — `rg` shows zero `max_len` left in `src/chats/`. The remaining hits fall into three buckets, none of which belong in the rename:

1. **`rename.py` `_AUTO_NAME_MAX_LENGTH` (+ its test)** — the 150-char cap on auto-generated *session names*. A different concept entirely; correctly untouched.
2. **`jsonl_scout.py` "Max len"** — a Rich table column header reporting field lengths. Display text, unrelated.
3. **`scripts/dev/truncate_json_strings.py`** — the interesting one: a standalone CLI whose `truncate_string` / `process_value` reimplement exactly what `truncate_middle` / `shorten_data` do (recursive middle-truncation of JSON string leaves).

On #3 — it *is* conceptual duplication, but I'd deliberately **leave it**, and not just out of caution:

- Every script in `scripts/dev/` (all five) is intentionally **stdlib-only** — none imports from the `chats` package, `scripts/` isn't even a package, and they're invoked as bare `python3 scripts/dev/…` (per the usage note in `can_we_parse_it.py`), not `uv run`. Importing `chats.utils` would couple a throwaway dev tool to the package against that established pattern, and might not even resolve the import the way it's actually run.
- Collapsing it would *change its output* — it uses a `...` placeholder and different split arithmetic than `truncate_middle`'s `\n...\n`.
- The drift it risks is harmless: it's a tool for eyeballing/shrinking fixtures, not something that must track the app's exact truncation.

So this "tetris block" is one where collapsing it would *add* coupling rather than remove complexity — the duplication is a cheap 20-line stdlib helper with no maintenance tie to the package. Its local `max_length` / `--max-length` naming is its own public interface and fine as-is; there's no `width` confusion to fix there.

Net: the rename is complete and correct in scope. If you'd nonetheless like that dev script folded onto `chats.utils` (accepting the coupling and the output change), say so and I'll do it — but my recommendation is to leave it standalone.
